31.quote_or_event: “Truth is higher than everything; but higher still is truthful living.”
31.explanation: In a Sri Raag ashtapadi Guru Nanak ranks sach aachaar, truthful conduct, above even the knowledge of Truth itself; the same hymn says that the companionship of the Naam brings the most excellent honour.
31.tie_back: Like Valluvar's rhetorical question, it names right living as the highest good a person can possess, the source of true honour.
31.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
31._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the supremacy of virtuous conduct, but the verse says nothing of worldly wealth, which Kural 31 explicitly claims virtue also yields.

32.quote_or_event: “In your mind, you do not remember the One Lord-you fool! You have forgotten the Lord; your virtues shall wither away.”
32.explanation: Guru Nanak pictures people sinking in a swamp of attachment and diagnoses their fall not as deliberate wickedness but as forgetting, warning that once God is forgotten, virtue itself withers.
32.tie_back: It shares the Kural's striking claim that the deepest ruin comes from forgetting rather than from open defiance.
32.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
32._accuracy_note: Close structural parallel (forgetting as the cause of ruin), though in Gurbani what is forgotten is God and the Name, whereas in the Kural it is aram itself.

33.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak! He knows the Path.”
33.explanation: In a salok that rejects holy men who live by begging, Guru Nanak defines the true path as honest labour and sharing from one's own earnings, the Sikh ideals of kirat karni and vand chhakna.
33.tie_back: Like Valluvar's 'by whatever means you are able', it measures the duty of doing good by what each person actually has and earns.
33.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Sarang (Sarang ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
33._accuracy_note: Good fit on giving according to one's own means, but the verse lacks the Kural's stress on doing good ceaselessly and in every situation.

34.quote_or_event: “Pilgrimages, austere discipline, compassion and charity - these, by themselves, bring only an iota of merit. Listening and believing with love and humility in your mind, cleanse yourself with the Name, at the sacred shrine deep within.”
34.explanation: In the Japji, Guru Nanak gives outward religious acts, even charity, only a sliver of worth, and locates true cleansing at an inner place of pilgrimage within the mind.
34.tie_back: Both texts make purity of mind the substance of religion and treat outward show as secondary noise.
34.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 4, Japji Sahib, Pauri 21, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
34._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on inner purity versus outward observance; the one difference is that the Japji attributes the cleansing to the Name, while the Kural speaks simply of a mind free from stain.

35.quote_or_event: “O anger, you are the root of conflict; compassion never rises up in you.” … “O greed, you cling to even the great, assaulting them with countless waves.”
35.explanation: In the Salok Sehskriti Guru Arjan addresses lust, anger, greed, attachment and ego one by one as personified enemies, the vices Sikh teaching calls the five thieves.
35.tie_back: Two of Valluvar's four faults, anger and greed, appear here as named forces that destroy compassion and right conduct.
35.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1358, Salok Sehskriti, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
35._accuracy_note: A reasonable but partial match: anger and greed correspond, but envy and harsh speech are not in this passage, and the five thieves are a different list from Valluvar's four.

36.quote_or_event: “Kabir! That which you have to do tomorrow - do it today instead; and that which you have to do now - do it immediately! Later on, you will not be able to do anything, when death hangs over your head.”
36.explanation: In one of his saloks preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib, the bhagat Kabir attacks procrastination, insisting that good be done at once because death leaves no time for it later.
36.tie_back: It is almost exactly Valluvar's rebuke of 'we will see to it when the time comes': do good now, before death arrives.
36.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1371, Salok Bhagat Kabir 138 (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
36._accuracy_note: Very close on the 'do it now' half; the Kural's second half (virtue as the undying companion at death) is matched in Gurbani by the Name, e.g. Sukhmani, Ang 264, and Kabir is a non-Sikh saint whose verses are part of Sikh scripture.

37.quote_or_event: “By His Command, some are high and some are low; by His Written Command, pain and pleasure are obtained.”
37.explanation: In the second stanza of the Japji, Guru Nanak traces every difference of high and low, pain and pleasure, to hukam, the divine order, and says that one who understands it no longer speaks in ego.
37.tie_back: Both texts read the visible gap between the fortunate and the burdened as the working of a moral order, though Gurbani assigns it to God's Command rather than to one's own past virtue alone.
37.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1, Japji Sahib, Pauri 2, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
37._accuracy_note: Only a partial parallel: Sikh teaching rejects caste and does not treat social rank as earned merit, so the verse shares the Kural's observation of inequality but not its argument that virtue visibly explains it.

38.quote_or_event: “This human body has been given to you. This is your chance to meet the Lord of the Universe. Nothing else will work.”
38.explanation: In this hymn from the evening Sodar liturgy, Guru Arjan presents human birth as a rare opportunity, warns that life spent in the love of Maya is squandered, and urges every effort to cross the world-ocean.
38.tie_back: Like the Kural's warning against letting a single day fall empty, it treats life's time as the chance to close the road of rebirth.
38.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
38._accuracy_note: Shares the urgency and the goal of release from rebirth, but the means in Gurbani is the Name and the company of the holy (sangat), not daily good deeds as such.

39.quote_or_event: “O Baba, the pleasures of other foods are false. Eating them, the body is ruined, and wickedness and corruption enter into the mind.”
39.explanation: In this Sri Raag hymn Guru Nanak sets the 'thirty-six flavours' found in love of the One against the pleasures of food, dress and riding, repeating in a refrain that all such pleasures are false and breed corruption.
39.tie_back: Like Valluvar, it denies the name of true pleasure to any enjoyment cut off from the right way, treating it as a source of harm.
39.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 16, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
39._accuracy_note: Good thematic fit, though Gurbani grounds true delight in love of God while the Kural grounds it in aram, and Sikhism, like the Kural, does not reject the householder's lawful pleasures.

40.quote_or_event: “Virtue and vice do not come by mere words; actions repeated, over and over again, are engraved on the soul. You shall harvest what you plant.”
40.explanation: In the Japji, Guru Nanak teaches that virtue and sin (punn and paap) are made by repeated deeds, which leave their mark on the self and bear their own fruit.
40.tie_back: Both close on the plain binary of good to be done and wrong to be avoided, judged by deeds rather than talk.
40.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 4, Japji Sahib, Pauri 20, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
40._accuracy_note: Strong fit on the virtue/vice binary defined by action, but the Kural frames what is to be avoided as public blame (pazhi), whereas the Japji frames it through karmic consequence under hukam.
